statement: As described in narrative reviews, some opioid painkillers have been reported with a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant in cases of serotonin toxicity, some of them fatal, and others have no reports. In a 2005 review by one author (Gillman), based on about 40 reports that are listed on his website and not in the paper, pethidine (meperidine), tramadol and dextromethorphan (a cough-medicine ingredient that he groups with these opioids) have definite reports with MAOIs, with fatalities named for each of the three (called possible for tramadol in one table), and possibly for fentanyl, which has one case and one possible death and is called uncertain; morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine have no reports. For methadone the review disagrees with itself: its abstract lists methadone among opioids involved in reactions with MAOIs, but its table says no reports are known, so methadone is not counted as reported here. He links this to how strongly each opioid blocks the serotonin transporter in laboratory tests (14.1 to 760 nM for pethidine, tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan; above 100,000 nM for the morphine group; lower is stronger; values from different sources and species); by the editors' reading, every value in the first group is above the 1 to 10 nM range he calls borderline. Boyer and Shannon (2005) state that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City resulted from pethidine (meperidine) with the MAOI phenelzine, citing a 1988 journal article whose title refers to the case, and list that pair first among seven combinations associated with severe serotonin syndrome; Buckley et al. (2014) list pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan among drugs associated with serotonin toxicity and say that nearly all severe cases involve an MAOI, a conclusion from reviews of case reports, four of the six by Gillman. Limits: nine of the eleven different papers Gillman cites for fatalities date from 1955 to 1971, and one of them is a rabbit study (editors' count); where their titles name an MAOI it is iproniazid, phenelzine (also as Nardil) or, in the rabbit study, pargyline, and none names moclobemide (editors' reading); he judges the old reports by his own reading; a 1968 test of pethidine and morphine in 15 patients (by its title, in the presence of MAOIs) found no serotonergic symptoms but did not look for clonus or reflexes; no rate is given and nobody counts the people who took an opioid with an MAOI without a problem; and no reports for the morphine group is an absence of reports, not a test in people. Gillman judges the risk with the serotonergic opioids probably low but unpredictable, says any reaction is dose-related, and says enzyme differences vary blood levels 20- to 50-fold between people. People can feel little pain relief from an amount of a painkiller for several reasons (a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, bodies that differ), and some take more; no source read measured what happens then with an MAOI.
plain: Reports link some opioid painkillers to serious reactions when taken with MAOI antidepressants. A 2005 review by one doctor says pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan (found in cough medicines) have been involved, some of them fatal, and that fentanyl is unclear. Methadone is unclear too: the review's summary lists it, but its own table says no reports are known. Morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine had no reports, which means a lack of reports, not a test in people. The review rests on about 40 reports it does not show; the papers it cites for deaths are mostly from 1955 to 1971; and nobody has counted how often the reaction happens. The doctor thinks the risk is probably low but unpredictable, and that it depends on the amount. Some people feel little pain relief from an amount and take more, for reasons such as a slow start, tolerance, a weaker or different product, a medicine that blunts it, or bodies that differ; no study measured what happens then with an MAOI.
population: People taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant who were given or took an opioid painkiller, as described in narrative reviews of case reports (about 40 on the main reviewer's website, not seen) and of laboratory measurements; his conclusion covers any type of MAOI, but the titles of the older fatality reports name iproniazid and phenelzine, not moclobemide
exposure: An opioid painkiller, or dextromethorphan, taken or given during MAOI treatment: pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, dextromethorphan, fentanyl, methadone; laboratory serotonin transporter values, Ki in nM (lower is stronger): pethidine 413, tramadol 760 and 528, dextromethorphan 23, methadone 270 and 14.1
comparator: Opioids that do not block the serotonin transporter appreciably (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine; values above 100,000 nM), for which no reports were found; there is no comparison in people
outcome: Reports of serotonin toxicity, some fatal, in published case reports as the main review counts and reads them; no rate
magnitude: No rate or relative risk is given in any source read. As described by Gillman (2005): about 40 reports of serotonin toxicity involving analgesics (list on the author's website, not seen). Serotonin transporter binding (Ki, nM; lower is stronger; values from different sources and species cannot be compared directly): morphine 500,000 and over 100,000; codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone over 100,000; pethidine 413; tramadol 760 and 528; dextromethorphan 23; methadone 270 and 14.1. Reports with MAOIs (his Table 2): morphine, codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone none; pethidine definite, with some fatalities; tramadol definite, with possible fatalities; dextromethorphan definite; fentanyl uncertain (one case and one possible death); remifentanil no case or death; pentazocine no reports known; methadone no reports known, but unlikely. Editors' count from the printed reference list: nine of the eleven different papers cited for fatalities are dated 1955 to 1971 (one is a rabbit study); the other two are from 1986 and 1992.

evidence.extracted: The abstract says the phenylpiperidine series opioids pethidine (meperidine), tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan, and propoxyphene, appear to be weak serotonin reuptake inhibitors and have all been involved in serotonin toxicity reactions with MAOIs (including some fatalities), and that morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be reuptake inhibitors and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs. It also says that only combinations of serotonergic drugs acting by different mechanisms can raise serotonin to a life-threatening level, and that the combination that most commonly does so is an MAOI with any reuptake inhibitor.

Table 2, serotonin transporter binding (Ki, nM; a lower value means higher potency; the caption says the values come from different sources and species and cannot be compared directly) and reports with MAOIs: morphine 500 000 (other references) and >100 000 (Codd), none; codeine, buprenorphine and oxycodone >100 000, none; tramadol 760 and 528, definite, and possible fatalities; dextromethorphan 23, definite; pethidine 413 weak, anomalous, definite, and some fatalities; pentazocine, no reports known; fentanyl, uncertain, one case of serotonin toxicity and one possible death reported; remifentanil, no case or death reported; methadone 270 and 14.1, no reports known, but unlikely. The Table 1 caption says fatalities from serotonin toxicity involving analgesics have been with pethidine, tramadol and dextromethorphan and, possibly, fentanyl.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning Overall, there is a strong association
evidence.extracted: The reviewer states that binding affinities at the serotonin transporter of less than 1 nM are invariably associated with the ability to precipitate toxicity with MAOIs and that potencies in the 1–10 nM range are borderline; that tramadol and venlafaxine are anomalous because their estimated potency suggests they should not be a risk, and that there is evidence they also act as serotonin releasers; and that pethidine, a very weak reuptake inhibitor, shows a large discrepancy that could possibly be accounted for by serotonin releasing properties, although there is no direct evidence. Editors' reading: every Table 2 value for pethidine, tramadol, methadone and dextromethorphan (14.1 to 760 nM) is above the 1–10 nM borderline range.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved (begins at the foot of p. 436 and continues on p. 437)
evidence.extracted: The reviewer says the early drugs involved in these interactions (pethidine and imipramine) are weak reuptake inhibitors and, because there is a dose–effect relationship, usually fail to produce a reaction. He describes a 1968 experiment (Evans-Prosser) in which 15 patients were given injections of pethidine, morphine or water in graduated doses in hospital, in blind random order (study condition: top single pethidine dose 75 mg, morphine 7.5 mg); none had serotonergic symptoms; reflexes and clonus were not examined, only pulse and arterial pressure. He reads this as confirming that weak reuptake inhibitors like pethidine are sometimes capable of precipitating toxicity, but only in susceptible individuals or with particularly large doses. He says the complete list of references on serotonin toxicity and analgesics, located through a search of the listed papers and standard databases (approximately 40), is on his website; that pethidine has undoubtedly caused a number of severe reactions and some fatalities, and the other reuptake-inhibiting analgesics also some fatalities; that a small series using usual therapeutic doses may lead to a false sense of security because the dose–effect relationship is not sufficiently appreciated; and that differences in cytochrome P450 enzymes produce 20–50-fold variations in serum levels between patients.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraphs beginning The limited available clinical and experimental data agree, Details of all cases involving analgesics and There are a few individual case reports (right-hand column)
evidence.extracted: The reviewer says the limited clinical and experimental data agree that morphine analogues (morphine, codeine, oxycodone, buprenorphine) are not reuptake inhibitors, none precipitates serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and there are no reports with them; that the phenylpiperidine opioids (pethidine, tramadol, methadone, fentanyl and congeners, dextromethorphan, propoxyphene) are probably all borderline, weak reuptake inhibitors, implicated in multiple reports that are almost certainly serotonin toxicity as judged by a subjective interpretation of the old case reports; that about 40 cases involving analgesics are in his updated review; and that all the opioid analgesics with serotonergic effects have been involved in serotonin toxicity reports but none of the drugs without reuptake-inhibiting capacity have. For fentanyl he judges one case report with a fatality (cardiac surgery in a patient on MAOIs) probably a result of serotonin toxicity and another possibly an unrecognised case, says there is a question mark over fentanyl, that it has probably been used in many unreported cases with MAOIs without a problem, and that there is insufficient basis for an accurate estimate of the risk.

The conclusion says morphine, codeine, oxycodone and buprenorphine are known not to be reuptake inhibitors and do not precipitate serotonin toxicity with MAOIs, and that pethidine, tramadol, dextromethorphan and methadone definitely are weak reuptake inhibitors and may infrequently precipitate dose-dependent serotonin toxicity with any type of MAOI, but perhaps only in large doses or susceptible individuals. The ability to estimate the risk is said to be compromised by a lack of systematically recorded clinical data and of precise potency data; for propoxyphene, pentazocine, fentanyl, remifentanil and congeners there are no reuptake affinity data, so interpolation and the presence or absence of clinical reports are used. The reviewer writes that the level of risk with known serotonergic opioids is probably low, but its unpredictable and serious nature makes it difficult to form judgments, and that any reaction is dose-dependent.

evidence.locator: Implicated drugs, paragraph beginning The early drugs that were involved, sentences on fatalities (p. 437); reference list, entries 14, 31, 48, 53, 57 to 60, 63, 64, 69 and 70 (pp. 440–441)
evidence.extracted: The sentences naming fatalities cite six papers for pethidine and six for the other reuptake-inhibiting analgesics, one paper appearing in both lists. The printed reference list shows reference 31 to be a study of fatal hyperthermia in rabbits, reference 60 to be titled as a paper on malignant hyperthermia with hypocalcaemia, reference 53 to be titled MAO inhibitors and coronary artery surgery: a patient death, and reference 14 (the 1968 experiment) to be titled The use of pethidine and morphine in the presence of monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Editors' reading of the titles of the eleven papers: where a title names an MAOI it is iproniazid, phenelzine (also under its brand name Nardil) or, in the rabbit study, pargyline; none names moclobemide. Editors' count from the printed reference list: of the eleven different papers cited for fatalities, nine date from 1955 to 1971 and two from 1986 and 1992.

The review states that the death of an 18-year-old patient in New York City more than 20 years earlier resulted from coadministration of meperidine (pethidine) and phenelzine (an MAOI) and calls it the most widely recognized example of this preventable condition. Its only support is reference 4, a 1988 article in the same journal whose title refers to the case itself; the review does not discuss how the cause of death was established.

evidence.locator: Definition and epidemiology, paragraph beginning A striking number of drugs and drug combinations (p. 1113); Table 1 (p. 1114)
evidence.extracted: The review says MAOIs that are irreversible or nonselective or that inhibit monoamine oxidase subtype A are strongly associated with severe cases of the syndrome, especially when used in combination with meperidine, dextromethorphan, SSRIs or MDMA. Its Table 1 lists the analgesics meperidine, fentanyl, tramadol and pentazocine among drugs associated with the syndrome, and phenelzine and meperidine as the first of seven combinations listed under drug interactions associated with severe serotonin syndrome, with no counts for any pair.

evidence.locator: Box 1 and its footnote; How do we diagnose it?, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Box 1 lists drugs associated with moderate to severe serotonin toxicity: among MAOIs, phenelzine, tranylcypromine, iproniazid, isocarboxazid, moclobemide, linezolid and methylene blue; and, among serotonin reuptake inhibitors, the opioid analgesics pethidine, tramadol, fentanyl and dextromethorphan. The footnote says severe toxicity generally involves a combination of agents from different drug classes. The text calls the serotonergic actions of drugs not marketed as serotonergic, such as tramadol and fentanyl, a trap for the unwary.

evidence.locator: How can we prevent it?, 2nd paragraph (beginning An awareness of drugs with potent serotonergic effects)
evidence.extracted: The review says it is apparent from systematic reviews of case reports (six references) that nearly all severe serotonin syndromes involve a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and that the relatively small number of these can easily be committed to memory. Editors' count from the reference list: four of the six cited reviews are by Gillman, one of them the 2005 review on opioids and MAOIs.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative reviews that did not appraise the underlying reports: the old reports are read against the modern definition by the reviewer's subjective interpretation; the count and nature of the fatalities cannot be checked from the paper (the case list is on a website, and a rabbit study and a paper titled on malignant hyperthermia are among the references for deaths); the 1968 experiment did not look for the signs in question.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: the opioid statements rest on one review, and the reviews that repeat them cite it. The methadone inconsistency within the review is stated in the claim.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the case reports, the 1968 experiment and the transporter measurements were not read; transporter values are indirect evidence for what happens in people.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review itself says that uneventful uses of fentanyl with MAOIs are probably unreported, so reports of problems may be over-represented.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the evidence is descriptive or consists of reports, and the rating is already at the floor (METHODS 6.3).

grade.reasoning: Case reports and laboratory values seen only through narrative reviews start from the design of the primary studies (observational reports: low) and are downgraded for risk of bias (not appraisable) and indirectness (second-hand) (METHODS 6.3): very low (the floor). The relation is worded as an association in reports: reports without a denominator cannot show that the opioids cause the reactions, and the reviewer himself says the basis for an accurate estimate of the risk is insufficient. Status single study: Gillman's review is the source of the opioid statements, Buckley et al. cite it among six reviews, and Boyer and Shannon's single-death statement rests on one 1988 article they cite without describing it, so the reviews do not count as independent. Stays draft: the claim rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3 and 12). The methadone statement follows the review's table and not its abstract. No advice in the sources is used.

verification.flag_note: Draft: rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3 and 12). Not read, and none has a reference record: the case reports behind Gillman's list (about 40, on www.psychotropical.com, a document he updates), the 1968 Evans-Prosser experiment (Br J Anaesth 40:279), Codd et al. 1995 (transporter values), the fentanyl reports (Noble 1992; Roy 2003), and the 1988 article Boyer and Shannon cite as reference 4 for the death of the 18-year-old (Asch and Parker, N Engl J Med 318:771-5; its type was not checked). The methadone inconsistency between Gillman's abstract and Table 2 is stated in the claim. Gillman's advice sentences (preferring opioids that are not reuptake inhibitors; treatment) and his remifentanil statements are not used. Literature after 2005 on opioids with MAOIs was not searched.
